hook.text: Every element absorbs specific wavelengths of light. By splitting starlight, we can identify what stars are made of.

buildup.text: Joseph Fraunhofer noticed dark lines in the Sun's spectrum in 1814. Each line corresponds to a chemical element.

discovery.text: Kirchhoff and Bunsen matched the lines to lab spectra in the 1860s, launching the field of astrophysics.

twist.text: Helium was discovered on the Sun before it was found on Earth. Its name comes from Helios—the Greek sun god.

climax.text: Today, spectroscopy reveals a star's composition, temperature, speed, and even whether it has planets.

punchline.text: Split the light, read the recipe. Every star reveals its secrets.

quiz.question: What can spectroscopy reveal about a star?
options: Its chemical composition, temperature, speed, and potential planets
Only whether it is a main sequence or giant star

details.summary: Spectroscopy — splitting light into its component wavelengths — revealed that stars are made of the same elements found on Earth. Each element produces a unique pattern of spectral lines, like a fingerprint.
details.whyItMatters: Spectroscopy transformed astronomy from mere position-tracking to understanding what celestial objects actually are. It proved that the same physics and chemistry apply everywhere in the universe — a profound realization.
takeaways: Spectroscopy splits light to reveal its component wavelengths
Each element produces unique spectral line fingerprints
It reveals composition, temperature, velocity, and magnetic fields

faq.question: How did spectroscopy prove stars contain familiar elements?
faq.answer: Joseph Fraunhofer discovered dark lines in the solar spectrum in 1814. By the 1860s, Kirchhoff and Bunsen showed these lines match elements studied in laboratories. The Sun's spectrum contains iron, hydrogen, calcium, and more — elements identical to those found on Earth.

faq.question: What is the Doppler effect in spectroscopy?
faq.answer: When a star moves toward us, its spectral lines shift toward blue (shorter wavelengths). Moving away, they shift toward red. This redshift/blueshift reveals how fast stars and galaxies are moving. It's how Hubble discovered the universe is expanding — distant galaxies are all redshifted.
